batch.title: Agroforestry: findings that move a rating (first check)
batch.notes: Every agroforestry finding that no person has checked yet and that would change a rating if it were wrong. Each card says what the paper says, what we recorded and what looks wrong (or that it checks out), and what Approve or Reject would change today (trial run, 10 Nov). The AI's suggested call shows under the buttons; it is a suggestion only. Approve = recorded correctly, stays in use. Hold = leave it open with a note. Reject = set aside (kept on record, no longer counted); pick a reason.

units.citation: Abdulai et al. (2017). Cocoa agroforestry is less resilient to sub‐optimal and extreme climate than cocoa in full sun. Global Change Biology.
units.quote:
During the extreme drought
of 2015/16, all cocoa plants under A. ferruginea died. Cocoa plants under A. toxicaria
suffered 77% mortality and massive stress with significantly reduced sap flux density
of 115 g cm2 day1, whereas cocoa in full sun maintained higher sap flux density
of 170 g cm2 day1. Moreover, cocoa sap flux recovery after the extreme drought
was significantly higher in full sun (163 g cm2 day1) than under A. toxicaria
(37 g cm2 day1). Soil water content in full sun was higher than in shaded systems
suggesting that cocoa mortality in the shaded systems was linked to strong competi-
tion for soil water.

relationship.outcome_raw: cocoa plant death, mortality and sap-flux stress during the El Nino extreme drought, cocoa under shade trees vs cocoa in full sun; mechanism: shade trees compete with cocoa for soil water (soil water lower under shade)

context.practice_as_described: 10-year-old cocoa plantation; cocoa shaded by individual Albizia ferruginea (recommended leguminous shade tree) or Antiaris toxicaria (most common shade tree) trees on a farmer field, vs adjacent cocoa without shade trees (full sun); no fertilizer, pesticides/fungicides applied to all plants
context.note: one farm, four replicate shade trees per species; study Nov 2014 - Mar 2016; the 2015/16 El Nino extremely dry period vs wet and normal-Harmattan dry periods (normal_year_reference = the wet/dry periods measured in the same plots); full-sun mortality not stated as a number; shade-tree species are part of the treatment (claim scoped to cocoa)

units.question: Abdulai 2017 says that in the 2015/16 extreme drought all cocoa under one shade-tree species died and 77% under another, while cocoa in full sun kept going. We recorded it as shade trees making drought damage to cocoa worse. Looks right. Approve keeps it. Reject: agroforestry drought protection for tree crops moves from 'conflicting' to 'low' (confidence medium to high), the same for shaded tree crops, and the one-paper shaded-crop drought row disappears. AI's view: Quote clearly shows higher drought mortality under shade than in full sun, recorded as harm.

units.citation: Biswas et al. (2022). Agroforestry offers multiple ecosystem services in degraded lateritic soils. Journal of Cleaner Production.
units.quote:
Simpson’s index of diversity was largest (0.62) in Gmelina- 
mango-pigeon pea and smallest (0.41) in pigeon pea (0.41), indicating 
respectively the maximum and minimum earthworm biodiversity.

relationship.outcome_raw: Simpson's diversity index of earthworms, Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea vs sole pigeon pea

context.practice_as_described: Gmelina arborea (forest tree, 400 plants/ha) + grafted mango (100 plants/ha) planted July 2009, with pigeon pea sown each year as an alley crop between the trees (agri-horti-silviculture); basal NPK 20:40:40 kg/ha to pigeon pea, prophylactic pesticide sprays on mango and Gmelina, need-based irrigation at tree establishment, prunings and leaf fall kept in the field; compared with sole pigeon pea (and sole Gmelina, sole mango) under rainfed conditions
context.note: Regional Research Station, Jhargram, West Bengal, India; degraded red and lateritic sandy loam; RCBD, 7 treatments x 3 replicates, 10 years (2009-10 to 2018-19); economics at a 12% discount rate, 1 USD = INR 62.72 (average 2009-19). The farming-system counterfactual used here is sole pigeon pea (T3); sole Gmelina and sole mango are forestry / orchard monocultures. Mechanism (p11): the multispecies agroforestry system gave a better microenvironment for soil fauna (litter inputs).

units.question: Adhikary 2022 says earthworm diversity was highest in the Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system (0.62) and lowest in sole pigeon pea (0.41). We recorded a strong biodiversity gain from trees among crops. Numbers are in the quote; no test of significance given, and it is earthworms only. Approve keeps it. Reject: agroforestry biodiversity drops from strong positive to slight positive (19 papers to 18), and the one-paper row for trees planted among crops disappears. AI's view: Numbers and comparison with sole pigeon pea are in the quote; note how much this one finding moves the headline rating.

units.quote:
The cost of production was the largest in the Gmelina-mango-pigeon 
pea system (482 USD ha−1 yr−1) compared to that for sole cultures [168,

relationship.outcome_raw: annual cost of production of the Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system (largest of all systems; inputs for tree, fruit-tree and crop components)

context.practice_as_described: Gmelina arborea (forest tree, 400 plants/ha) + grafted mango (100 plants/ha) planted July 2009, with pigeon pea sown each year as an alley crop between the trees (agri-horti-silviculture); basal NPK 20:40:40 kg/ha to pigeon pea, prophylactic pesticide sprays on mango and Gmelina, need-based irrigation at tree establishment, prunings and leaf fall kept in the field; compared with sole pigeon pea (and sole Gmelina, sole mango) under rainfed conditions
context.note: Regional Research Station, Jhargram, West Bengal, India; degraded red and lateritic sandy loam; RCBD, 7 treatments x 3 replicates, 10 years (2009-10 to 2018-19); economics at a 12% discount rate, 1 USD = INR 62.72 (average 2009-19). The farming-system counterfactual used here is sole pigeon pea (T3); sole Gmelina and sole mango are forestry / orchard monocultures. Cost of cultivation averaged per year over the 10-year cycle; inputs listed in the paper's Table S1 (seedlings/grafts, fertiliser, manure, pesticide, diesel, irrigation, labour, machinery) - mixes establishment and recurrent items, so cost_nature left out.

units.question: Adhikary 2022 says the Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system cost 482 USD per ha per year, against 168 for sole pigeon pea. We recorded a cost of 482. That is the total cost, not the extra over pigeon pea (about 314), and it mixes set-up and running costs. Approve keeps it. Reject: the running-cost row for agroforestry stays unrated but confidence falls from medium to very low; the one-paper rows for trees among crops and shaded tree crops disappear. AI's view: The cost figure is in the quote and correctly read; total rather than extra cost is a known limitation.

band.value: an absolute value of 482 usd per ha yr
band.basis: ORDINAL cost class — 'is this a big or small amount given the context' (Pete 2026-10-05; no currency/price-year normalisation). Thresholds are scoping-grade, set against a typical LMIC smallholder gross margin of roughly USD 200–800/ha/yr; UMIC thresholds ×2, HIC ×5. slight = small · moderate · strong = large. Adjust the thresholds, not the mechanism.

units.citation: Ashraf et al. (2019). Alley-cropping system increases vegetation heterogeneity and moderates extreme microclimates in oil palm plantations. Agricultural and Forest Meteorology.
units.quote:
The amelioration of harsh microclimatic effects in some of the crops
the alley-cropping system is possibly due to the greater leaf area, in-
creased transpiration, lower light penetration and reduced wind speed
experienced in the majority of alley-cropping treatments. Fifteen year
old oil palm is likely to have a higher relative humidity due to the
closed canopy, whereas seven year old oil palm experiences greater
sunlight penetration due to the more open canopy structure (Corley and
Tinker, 2003). Luskin and Potts (2011) stated that young oil palm trees
experienced greater fluctuations in local climate condition compared to
mature trees due to their less complex canopy and lower leaf area
index, explaining the greater light intensity in seven year old oil palm
monoculture. This highlights the potential benefits of applying the alley
cropping system in young oil palm stands as it can ameliorate these
effects. In addition, some alley-cropping treatments improved soil
moisture, which is a limiting factor on oil palm yield (Tao et al., 2017).

context.practice_as_described: silvopastoral systems (SPS) combining pastures, trees and livestock on the same unit of land: SPS in native forests with natural grasslands, SPS in native forests with pasture implantation, SPS with forest plantations of exotic tree species and cultivated pastures, and SPS with forest plantations in natural grasslands; compared with surrounding grasslands/pastures without trees
context.note: Annual forage dry-matter production (AFP) from manual quadrat cuts in closure cages, SPS vs adjacent treeless grassland/pasture (100% light transmissivity), two-factor ANOVA (system x year type). Authors' definition (p7): a dry year is annual rainfall more than 35% below the site's long-term mean; a normal year is less than that. Pooled across sites spanning semi-arid to very humid (aridity index 14-66), tree canopy cover 16.8-82.4%, so no single climate_zone. Grouping by drought-intensity category is shown in Fig. 2B; the text does not print the letters' significance, so significance is not_reported. HARM finding kept: under severe drought the treeless system out-yields the silvopasture. Quoted from the abstract; results (p10: 'an oppositive response was observed under more severe drought intensities (> 35%) determining a competition process with the presence of trees') and discussion (p11, p14) restate this reversal ('more severe droughts (> 35%) the response was the reverse'). The cut-off is a rainfall deficit relative to the 30-year mean, not an author severity scale.

context.practice_as_described: Cacao agroforestry (AF) in a long-term randomised field trial at Sara Ana, Alto Beni, Bolivia: cacao (625 trees/ha) planted under shade trees - mainly Inga and Erythrina, plus timber, fruit and palm trees, 304 shade trees/ha - with plantain as a by-crop, replaced by banana in the agroforestry plots from 2012 (p3). BASELINE (comparator): full-sun cacao monoculture (cacao + plantain until end-2011, then cacao alone). Both arms were run under organic and under conventional management (agroforestry conventional 'Afc', agroforestry organic 'Afo', monoculture conventional 'Mc', monoculture organic 'Mo'); the AF-vs-mono contrast pools the two managements. Agroforestry plots received HALF the fertiliser / compost dose of the monocultures by design (p3). First 5 years after establishment (data 2010-2014); timber revenue not counted (p3). Mechanism (authors, p4): lower light incidence and lower tree vigour under shade reduce cacao yield.
context.note: Fig. 2a 'Mean ± standard error of the a cacao and b plantain ... yields in the four production systems' (p5). Contrast estimate AF vs mono -52.3 ± 5.3 (P < 0.001), in the quote. Cacao began producing in 2011 (3 years after planting), so this is young-plantation yield. Authors' caveat in the same paragraph (p4): the AF-vs-mono gap was mainly driven by the conventional monoculture - organic monoculture yielded 48% less than conventional monoculture, while organic and conventional agroforestry yielded similarly (P = 0.16); the agroforestry arm also got half the fertiliser dose. 2014 was a regional low-yield year ('unfavorable weather conditions', p4) - not named as a drought, so no hazard tag (#38). Plantain/banana yields (Fig. 2b, higher in AF, P < 0.001) left out as a separate unit: banana was planted only in the AF arm by design, so the by-crop effect is carried by the revenue unit.

units.question: Armengot 2016 says full-sun cacao gave 41% more than cacao under shade trees. We recorded a strong yield loss from shade. Reject: yields for shaded tree crops stay 'conflicting' but confidence rises from medium to high. AI's view: Direction and significance are in the quote; the fertiliser difference is part of the trial design, worth knowing.

units.quote: La présence des arbres protège contre le vent, atténue l’érosion, et l’évaporation et enrichit le sol à travers la décomposition de la litière mais également à partir des nutriments apportés par les animaux qui se réfugient à l’ombre des arbres. (English: The presence of trees protects against the wind, reduces erosion and evaporation, and enriches the soil through the decomposition of litter but also through the nutrients brought by the animals that shelter in the shade of the trees.)

context.practice_as_described: Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR; French 'régénération naturelle assistée', RNA): farmers protect and manage the natural regrowth (shoots) produced by living tree and shrub stumps in their cropped fields - select the shoots to keep, cut the others, prune the kept stems every year and harvest branches for fodder, wood and organic matter (section 'Le principe et fondement de la RNA'); occasionally enriched by direct seeding of useful species. Not planted trees. Maradi and Zinder regions, Niger: parklands of 20 to 80 trees/ha, often dominated by Faidherbia albida (Zinder). BASELINE: fields without regenerated trees (implicit).

units.quote: La RNA permet ainsi de réduire la vulnérabilité des ménages pendant les périodes difficiles. units.quote:
L’augmentation du nombre d’arbres dans les champs de culture s’est traduite dans beaucoup de 
cas par une forte réduction du temps nécessaires pour sa collecte.  Dans les zones reverdies au 
Niger il fallait il y a 20 ans en moyenne 2,5 heures/jour pour la collecte de bois de chauffe pour 
couvrir les besoins d’une famille, mais à présent il ne faut que 0,5 heure/jour. (English: The increase in the number of trees in cropped fields has in many cases translated into a strong reduction in the time needed for its [firewood] collection. In the re-greened zones of Niger, 20 years ago an average of 2.5 hours/day was needed to collect firewood to meet a family's needs, but now only 0.5 hour/day is needed.)

Encoded on gender_inequity (women's labour burden falls); the time saved let women develop other income-generating activities (same page). Strength from the with/without ratio (lower is better for a burden).

units.quote:
It is now well recognized that trees can enrich soil
conditions in agroforestry systems through various
biological processes and mechanisms including in-
crease in soil organic matter content from ﬁne root
sloughing and litterfall, increased soil N through N2
ﬁxation Nair et al. 1999; Nygren et al. 2000,
changes in soil chemical, physical, and biological
properties by meso and micro fauna around roots, and
enhancement of the total nutrient pool by faunal
droppings Belsky et al. 1993; Tornquist et al. 1999;
Wedderburn and Carter 1999. In a long-term study
in semiarid northeastern Brazil, the presence of two
native tree species, Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias
tuberosa, in pastures of varied conditions were shown
to signiﬁcantly increase available P and total C, and
increase exchangeable K by 50% Wick et al. 2000.

The review describes the mechanism as litterfall and fine-root sloughing adding soil organic matter, nitrogen fixation, and animal droppings adding nutrients.

Retained trees in pasture rather than planted silvopasture. The 'long-term' study duration is not given in the review. P = phosphorus, K = potassium, C = carbon.

units.citation: Ehui et al. (1990). Economic analysis of soil erosion effects in alley cropping, no-till and bush fallow systems in South Western Nigeria. Agricultural Systems.
units.quote:
Annual labor requirements for maize production under the soil 
management technologies are according to Ngambeki (1985). Eighty-two 
man-days are required for the 6-year cycle traditional fallow management 
system with 50 percent farming intensity. In the 4 m alley cropping system, 
annual labor use is increased by 53 percent due to added labor for hedgerow 
pruning.

relationship.outcome_raw: annual labour use (man-days) for maize production, 4 m Leucaena alley cropping vs 6-year cycle bush fallow

context.practice_as_described: continuous-cultivation maize alley cropping with Leucaena leucocephala hedgerows planted at 4 m interhedgerow spacing, hedgerows periodically pruned (about 20% of the land occupied by trees per the authors)
context.note: Comparator = the authors' control, traditional bush fallow with 3-year cropping in a 6-year cycle (50% farming intensity). Other arms in the same model: no-till with herbicide, and 3-year cropping in a 12-year cycle bush fallow. Simulation: SCUAF (simplified USLE) erosion over a 20-year horizon for a sandy Oxic Paleustalf, 7% slope, seeded with IITA Ibadan plot erosion rates (Kang and Ghuman 1989; Sabel-Koschella et al. 1984); maize yield from Lal (1981) yield-cumulative-soil-loss function. Mechanism: hedgerows lower erosion through a tree proportionality factor in SCUAF (degree to which erosion is controlled by the tree component); lower cumulative soil loss sustains maize yield; pruning raises labour. Harm/cost tail kept: added labour for hedgerow pruning. Labour requirements taken from Ngambeki (1985) per the authors. Labour is a recurring operating cost; the paper prices it at a wage rate (Table 1).

units.question: Kang 1990 says maize alley cropping with Leucaena needed 53% more labour a year than bush fallow, for hedge pruning. We recorded a cost increase. Looks right; the labour figure is from an earlier study. Approve keeps it. Reject: the cost row for agroforestry stays unrated, confidence high to medium. AI's view: The 53% extra labour is in the quote.

units.citation: Kim et al. (2016). Carbon sequestration and net emissions of CH4 and N2O under agroforestry: Synthesizing available data and suggestions for future studies. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment.
units.quote:
Net soil CH4 emissions were
reduced (i.e. more CH4 oxidation) when agriculture was shifted to
improved fallow, slash-and-burn systems and tree plantations on
arable land, but increased with a change to shaded perennial-crop
systems (Table 5).
Any reduced net CH4 emissions in agroforestry (i.e. greater
uptake) compared with agriculture (as seen for improved fallow,
slash-and-burn systems, and tree plantations on arable land) was
probably mainly related to greater soil pore space in soils under
agroforestry compared with agricultural ﬁelds, as reﬂected in
reduced soil bulk density under agroforestry (Table 5). Since
diffusion of CH4 into the soil has been proposed as the primary
constraint on CH4 oxidation rates (Dobbie and Smith, 1996; Ball
et al., 1997; Priemé et al., 1997; Christiansen and Gundersen, 2011),
the larger soil pore space under agroforestry may be the primary
reason for enhanced CH4 oxidation rates.
It has also been observed that CH4 uptake rates of soils can be
reduced by application of ammonium-N fertilizer because it has
been shown at the enzymatic level that NH4
+ can strongly inhibit
CH4 oxidation rates (Steudler et al., 1989; King, 1997; Topp and
Pattey, 1997; Le Mer and Roger, 2001; Dutaur and Verchot, 2007).
CH4 oxidation rates under agricultural ﬁelds may thus be further
reduced by exposure to often excessive N fertilizer applications.
The difference in CH4 oxidation was relatively small in shaded
perennial crop systems (Table 5), and the growth of N-ﬁxing trees
in these systems (Makumba et al., 2006; Akinnifesi et al., 2007,
2010) may provide N at levels where it can inhibit CH4 oxidation in
the soil.

relationship.outcome_raw: net soil CH4 emission higher (less CH4 oxidation) after a shift from agriculture to shaded perennial-crop systems; N from N-fixing shade trees may inhibit CH4 oxidation

context.note: Global data synthesis: 109 observations from 56 publications for biomass/soil C change and 26 data sets from 15 publications for CH4/N2O (agroforestry vs adjacent agriculture). Unweighted means with 95% CI; few below-ground measurements (root:shoot 0.3 assumed). Minus signs and plus/minus symbols are missing from the PDF text layer. Reversal for the shaded perennial family (few observations). The same passage reports lower net CH4 under improved fallow, slash-and-burn and tree plantations on arable land, attributed to greater soil pore space; those are rotational / plantation types outside the type 1 families and are not emitted.

context.note: measured drop is clear; the cause is hedged by the authors ('possibly due to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year'); right next to the belt (0.01-0.05) water rose again, probably from trapped snow; supports the competition-for-water mechanism of kowa95_1

units.question: Kowalchuk 1995 says soil water dropped close to the shelterbelt in 1990, 'possibly' because the trees took it up; in 1989 the pattern ran the other way. We recorded windbreaks drying the soil. Doubtful: it compares near-belt with mid-field in one year, not fields with vs without belts, and the cause is a guess. Approve keeps it. Reject: the one-paper water shortage row for windbreaks and hedges ('slight negative') disappears; in high-income countries the agroforestry water shortage line goes from 'slight negative' to 'conflicting'. AI's view: One-year within-field gradient with a hedged cause and an opposite year is thin ground for a with-vs-without effect.

context.practice_as_described: juvenile plumcot trees (planted 2019, rows 5 m apart) intercropped with soybean (wide-narrow rows 1.2 m from the trees, sown each spring) or alfalfa (rows 0.15 m apart, 1.0 m from the trees, sown with the trees); all treatments drip-irrigated and fertilised (DAP, potassium sulphate, urea, water-soluble fertiliser), intercropped soybean at a lower seeding rate and irrigation amount than sole soybean
context.note: Field experiment, Yili (Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture), Xinjiang, China, 2020-2021, 30 x 24 m plots, three replicates; treatments plumcot+soybean (PSI), plumcot+alfalfa (PAI), sole soybean (SS), sole alfalfa (SA), sole plumcot (SP). Yields per unit of total plot area. Plus a farm-household survey (not extracted). Currency EUR as printed. Mechanism (p7, p1): fruit and legume/forage output from the same land (LER above one) lets the system earn while the trees are juvenile. Against sole plumcot the intercrop gain is the crop revenue; against sole crops it is the fruit revenue.

relationship.outcome_raw: maize grain yield (t per ha) in season S95/96: maize under dispersed Grevillea trees vs unshaded sole maize; different letters = significant difference

context.practice_as_described: CIRUS (Complementarity In Resource Use on Sloping land) trial, ICRAF Machakos Research Station, semi-arid Kenya. Treatment CTd: dispersed Grevillea robusta trees planted in October 1991 on the contour at 3 m x 4 m (833 trees per ha), pruned to single stems (leaf area index 0.25-0.50), with maize (Katumani composite) grown continuously as an understorey crop at sole-crop density from 1994; no fertiliser or residues; a contour vetiver grass strip crossed every plot; root trenches 1 m deep cut round the plots each season against roots from neighbouring plots (pp1-2). BASELINE (comparator): Cg 0% = unshaded sole maize at the same density. The trial also had sole maize under 25% and 50% artificial shade nets (Cg 25%, Cg 50%); these nets mimic shade and are NOT the practice, so they are not used as a comparator or treatment here (catalogue #38c).
context.note: Table 1 'Seasonal rainfall, above-ground biomass and grain yield for maize grown under 0, 25 and 50% artificial shade (Cg 0%, Cg 25% and Cg 50%) or in the CTd agroforestry system' (p4). Row order: season, rainfall (mm), above-ground biomass t/ha for Cg 0%, Cg 25%, Cg 50%, CTd, then grain yield t/ha for Cg 0%, Cg 25%, Cg 50%, CTd; values in a season followed by different letters differ at P < 0.05. Only the grain-yield Cg 0% vs CTd pair is encoded; biomass and the shade-net columns are left out (biomass is not a yield outcome; nets mimic the practice). Season: 1995/96 short rains, 317 mm; the authors name a 'sustained drought in S95/96' (p8). Balanced incomplete block design, four replicates, 20 m x 20 m plots; trees 3-5 years old in these seasons. Mechanism (authors, p9): understorey maize flowered 5 days later in the wet season but 15-24 days later in seasons when flowering came after available soil moisture was depleted, 'resulting in crop failure'; because artificial shade of similar intensity delayed flowering by at most 5 days, the delay and yield loss are attributed to below-ground competition for water with the trees, which outweighed the benefit of cooler temperatures. Supersedes the second-hand reading in ev_crop_yield_watts22_10.

Reject: drought protection for rainfed cropping goes from 'conflicting' to 'moderate' (11 papers), and for trees among crops also to 'moderate'. context.note: Results 3.2 and Figure 1 'Seasonal mean diurnal timecourses of meristem temperature ... in the CTd agroforestry system' (p4); the text layer prints the degree sign as '8C'. The cooling weakened in later seasons (L95, S95/96) as the trees grew taller and lower branches were pruned, letting air flow under the canopy (p4, p7) - a weakening service, not a harm. Despite the cooling, yield fell under the trees (ev_crop_yield_lott09_1 to _4): below-ground competition outweighed the microclimate benefit (abstract, p1).

units.citation: Ma et al. (2020). Carbon accumulation in agroforestry systems is affected by tree species diversity, age and regional climate: A global meta‐analysis. Global Ecology and Biogeography.
units.quote:
Conversion from cropland to AFS generally increased SOC stor-
age, consistent with previous findings (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Shi 
et al., 2018). However, conversion from pastures to AFS did not af-
fect SOC stocks, which is consistent with Laganière et al. (2010) and 
Poeplau et  al.  (2011), who found no impact on SOC stocks when 
grasslands were afforested. This is probably attributable to the 
higher belowground capacity for biomass C production of peren-
nial pastures (Baritz et al., 2010), particularly in relationship to an-
nual cropland (Baah-Acheamfour et al., 2015), and the fact that soil 
C stocks are strongly affected by grass biomass inputs even after 
introducing trees into pastures (Upson, Burgess, & Morison, 2016).

relationship.outcome_raw: soil organic carbon stock when cropland is converted to agroforestry (trees added to cropland) vs adjacent cropland; mechanism: tree litter and root inputs on soils depleted by annual cropping

context.practice_as_described: tree-based agroforestry systems (trees integrated with crops or pastures in the same land-use unit: windbreaks, alley cropping, hedgerows, shelterbelts and other tree-based systems; shrub-based systems excluded) compared with adjacent sole cropland or pasture without trees
context.note: global meta-analysis of paired agroforestry vs adjacent cropland/pasture observations (mixed models, study as random effect, replication-weighted); no country list in the paper text; mixed-species vs single-species and tree-age moderators not extracted (design moderators, not practice vs counterfactual); subgroup of the pooled SOC result (previous land use = cropland)

context.practice_as_described: Four coffee (Coffea arabica) plantation types on smallholder farms, typed a priori by the botanical make-up of the shade canopy: C1 = coffee in full sun (no shade canopy); C2 = coffee with bananas/plantains (musaceae) and service shade trees (some nitrogen-fixing legumes, mainly Inga spp.); C3 = coffee with service trees and timber trees (Cordia alliodora, Cedrela odorata); C4 = coffee with service trees, timber trees, fruit trees (Citrus, mango, avocado) and musaceae. 27 farms (26.2 ha) in El Cua, El Tuma-La Dalia, Jinotega and Rancho Grande, north-central Nicaragua (4 C1, 8 C2, 8 C3, 7 C4); mean plantation age 8 years, mean shade 44%; conventional management in all types (fungicides, soil and foliar fertiliser, insecticides or berry-borer traps, shade-tree regulation, coffee pruning, chemical and manual weeding) (pp23-24). THIS UNIT: C4 (coffee under service, timber and fruit trees plus musaceae; C3 values also given). BASELINE (comparator): C1, unshaded full-sun coffee.
context.note: Table 6 (Cuadro 6, p31) 'Yields of agroforestry products in four coffee-plantation types in north-central Nicaragua'; the caption and footnote sit at the top of p31 and the table body after Table 7 in the text layer, so only the header and the coffee row are quoted. Footnote: different letters along a row = significant difference (LSD Fisher, p<0.05); qq = quintal (100 lb, 45.4 kg) of green coffee (cafe oro). Only C2 vs C4 differed (p30: 'solo existio diferencia significativa entre C2 y C4'); no shaded type differs from full sun (C1 'ab'). Yields are farmer-reported max/min/mode via semi-structured interview, fitted to a triangular distribution (p25); production year 2013. Yield variance was larger in C1 and C2 (p30), which the author links to the stronger biennial bearing of little-shaded coffee (p36). Rows left out: firewood, bananas, citrus, other fruit and standing timber, which have no full-sun value (N/A) and were not tested. Mechanism (author, p28 and p14): coffee bushes in full sun are more vigorous (coffee basal area 19.56 m2/ha in C1 vs 8.37-11.37 in shaded types, Table 4, p29) and shade reduces flower-bud numbers (DaMatta 2004, cited p14).

units.question: Pinoargote 2014 (Nicaragua) reports coffee yields of 22.1 under the most diverse shade vs 37.7 in full sun (quintals/ha), but the letters show no clear difference, and banana-shaded coffee gave 38.8, slightly above full sun. We recorded a strong loss. 'Strong' looks too much for a non-significant gap that picks one shade type. Approve keeps it. Reject: the separate low- and lower-middle-income yields line (strong positive, 48 papers) would no longer show, as it would then match the overall rating; that evidence is not lost. AI's view: Strength set to strong on a non-significant difference while another shade type showed no loss.

context.note: Table 7 (Cuadro 7, p31); see ev_economic_return_pinoar14_1 for the rows quoted. In-kind cost (costo en especie, CS) = the money value of FAMILY labour (p26); cash costs (CE) cover fungicides, fertilisers, insecticides, berry-borer traps, coffee transport and hired labour. This is an annual operating cost of the whole coffee plot, not an establishment cost of the trees. Shaded types use more family labour (C2 693 a, C3 271 ab, C4 498 a vs C1 54 b); the author (p32) says the high family labour in C2 drives its negative net income from other agroforestry products (Figure 4B), and (p38) that a family work-day on the shaded plot pays more than off-farm day labour. Total cost (cash + in-kind) is similar across types (C1 1807, C4 1686 US$/ha/yr by addition of Table 7 values; computed here, not stated by the author).

units.question: Pinoargote 2014 shows family-labour cost of 498 US$/ha under diverse shade coffee vs 54 in full sun (significant), but cash costs were lower (1188 vs 1753, no clear difference), so total cost was about equal or lower. We recorded a higher running cost, which misses the cash side. Approve keeps 'higher cost'. Reject: running cost for agroforestry overall drops to one paper; the rows for trees among crops and shade-tree crops disappear. AI's view: Labour cost rose but cash cost fell in the same table, so 'higher cost' is one-sided.

relationship.outcome_raw: wheat grain yield (t per ha), research plot with tree strips vs adjacent waterlogged fields without plantation (3.4 times); attributed to the lowered water table letting rainwater percolate, relieving oxygen deficiency in the wheat root zone

context.practice_as_described: Biodrainage agroforestry model: four parallel strip plantations of clonal Eucalyptus tereticornis (Mysore gum, clone C-7) planted in December 2002 on raised ridges (0.5 m high) built along the field bunds of canal-irrigated, waterlogged farmers' fields at Puthi, Hisar, Haryana (northwest India). Strips were 66 m apart, each with two tree rows at 1 m x 1 m (300 plants per ha; 240 surviving); the strips occupied about 4% of the area and wheat was grown in the remaining 96% between them (p2). The deep-rooted, high-water-use trees act as 'bio-pumps' that transpire groundwater and lower the water table. BASELINE (comparator): adjacent canal-irrigated waterlogged fields without plantation (control observation wells 1 and 11; four untreated wheat fields).
context.note: Figure 5 'Wheat yield obtained with and without Eucalyptus plantation' (p7). Single season (wheat sown November 2007, harvested April 2008), quadrat (1 m x 1 m) sampling; no statistical test reported. Sowing in the untreated fields was delayed by one to two weeks by wetter soil (p3), part of the pathway. The plot-level figure already nets out the 11.7% decline near the tree lines (see ev_crop_yield_ram11_3). Supersedes the second-hand reading in ev_crop_yield_singhlal18_2.

units.quote:
The farming methods also affected food sufﬁciency.
Improved agroforestry was securing enough food
throughout the year for 40% of the households. The
amount was only 18% in households using traditional
practices, notwithstanding they are cultivating mainly
food crops.

relationship.outcome_raw: share of households with enough food throughout the year, improved agroforestry vs traditional cultivation

context.practice_as_described: 'improved agroforestry systems': land use well planned, multipurpose trees (many nitrogen-fixing) planted as windbreaks, shelterbelts or around fields, intercropped with annual crops or in alley farming, densely cultivated annual and perennial crops enriched with well-managed cash crops (cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves), manure used where cattle are kept; compared with traditional slash-and-burn / short-fallow cultivation with few trees
context.note: Household survey (154 randomly sampled households, 4 villages in the buffer zone of Amani Nature Reserve, East Usambara, Tanzania, 2001) plus PRA; farms classified improved vs traditional by observation (Table 3). Not randomised: improved farms are larger, mostly in the highlands, keep more dairy cattle and have more off-farm income; net income regression shows land size, tenure, cash crops, dairy and off-farm income as drivers (Table 5). USD at TZS 876.4 (Nov 2001). Mechanism (p7): higher year-round income from cash crops and livestock; livestock income stabilised food sufficiency outside the harvest season - partly a dairy effect within the bundle.

units.question: Reyes 2005 (Tanzania) says 40% of households with improved agroforestry had enough food all year vs 18% with traditional farming. We recorded better food security. context.practice_as_described: Silvopasture on degraded rocky rangeland at the Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) Range Management and Soil Conservation Centre, Bhopalgarh, Jodhpur district, Rajasthan: seven multipurpose tree and shrub species (MPTS) - Acacia tortilis, Acacia senegal, Azadirachta indica (neem), Hardwickia binata, Albizia lebbek, and the shrubs Dichrostachys nutans and Colophospermum mopane - planted in pits at 10 x 4 m spacing in 1985 (each pit refilled with soil plus farmyard manure, 10 L water per irrigation in the first two years), grass in the interspaces (Cenchrus setigerus, Dichanthium annulatum, Aristida funiculata) cut at maturity; randomised block design, three replicates, trees 14 and 15 years old at measurement (p2). Drought years 1999 and 2000 (annual rainfall about 260 mm each, against a 360 mm mean, 'highly erratic and caused drought during both the years', p2); good-rainfall reference years 1995 and 1996 taken from Singh (2000). Mechanism (authors, p4): trees compete with the understorey grass for moisture during drought years and shade it, so tree presence did not buffer the drought loss of herbage.
context.note: Table 3 (p6), last column 'Reduction in herbage production (%) due to drought': 48-65% under the seven tree/shrub species vs 47% under the control without trees. The good-rainfall reference years (1995-96) come from the authors' earlier publication (Singh 2000), not the same seasons. Herbage only: tree top-feed produced in the drought year is not counted here. context.practice_as_described: Silvopasture on degraded rocky rangeland at the Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) Range Management and Soil Conservation Centre, Bhopalgarh, Jodhpur district, Rajasthan: seven multipurpose tree and shrub species (MPTS) - Acacia tortilis, Acacia senegal, Azadirachta indica (neem), Hardwickia binata, Albizia lebbek, and the shrubs Dichrostachys nutans and Colophospermum mopane - planted in pits at 10 x 4 m spacing in 1985 (each pit refilled with soil plus farmyard manure, 10 L water per irrigation in the first two years), grass in the interspaces (Cenchrus setigerus, Dichanthium annulatum, Aristida funiculata) cut at maturity; randomised block design, three replicates, trees 14 and 15 years old at measurement (p2). Drought years 1999 and 2000 (annual rainfall about 260 mm each, against a 360 mm mean, 'highly erratic and caused drought during both the years', p2); good-rainfall reference years 1995 and 1996 taken from Singh (2000). Mechanism (in the quote): the trees and shrubs are lopped for green leaf fodder in drought years, when grass is scarce; the treeless pasture has no such browse layer. Authors' conclusion (p6): 'herbage as well as top feed production is possible during drought years for sustainable livestock production'.
context.note: Table 2 'Top feed production from 14 year old trees and shrubs' (p5): dry leaf fodder 0.08-1.85 t/ha by species (A. tortilis 1.21, A. senegal 1.01, A. indica 0.87, D. nutans 1.85 t/ha), measured in 1999, a drought year, after pruning one third of the lower crown (p2, p4). The comparator is implicit (control pasture has no tree layer) - the paper never sums top feed and herbage against the control, so no magnitude is encoded. JUDGEMENT CALL for review: kept as low-confidence direction evidence so that the trade-off (less grass, plus browse) is not reported one-sidedly.

units.question: van Noordwijk 2021 summarises another review (Bayala 2015): in Sahel parklands, tree roots lift deep soil water that crop roots can then use. We recorded this as better soil water holding that protects against drought. It is second-hand, describes how it might work, measures no effect, and moving water is not the same as holding it. Approve keeps it. Reject: natural regrowth on farmland stays 'very high' for drought protection, confidence falls from very high to high. AI's view: A second-hand description of how trees move water, with nothing measured, should not count as soil water holding or a drought vote.

units.quote:
As for financial profitability, Hybrid shade had by far the 
highest average plot profitability with value of production at 669±565 
USD ha−1 yr−1 VOP – 65% higher than the average for Hybrid sun.

relationship.outcome_raw: value of production (revenues from cocoa, intercrops, fruit, fuelwood and timber minus input and hired-labour costs, USD/ha/yr), moderate-shade vs full/near-full-sun hybrid cocoa

context.practice_as_described: Hybrid (series II) cocoa under moderate shade, 13-25 shade trees per ha of >30 cm DBH (Hybrid shade, n=30 plots, mean 22 shade trees/ha), compared with hybrid cocoa under full or near-full sun (Hybrid sun, <=6 shade trees/ha, n=50, mean 0.4). Smallholder plots in Kwaebibirem and Atiwa West, mixed with fruit trees and annual food crops on some plots; management (fertiliser, pruning, weeding, hand pollination) varies within both systems and is not held constant.
context.note: 2021 plot survey of 106 farms (30 x 30 m sub-plots); systems stratified by shade-tree density then clustered by management. Shade is NOT randomised: fertiliser, cocoa density and pollination differ between and within systems, so the shade contrast is confounded. The third system (Amazonia variety under moderate shade) differs by variety and is not used as a shade contrast here. Ordinal economics only (no currency normalisation). Mechanism (section 4.4): higher and less variable cocoa yield across clusters, plus some diversified revenue; costs were similar across systems (means about 144 vs 150 USD/ha/yr). 95% CIs are wide and overlap (669 +/- 565 vs 404 +/- 442); cocoa price was the most sensitive parameter. VOP omits land rent and post-harvest marketing costs.

units.question: Hawkins 2024 (Ghana) says cocoa under moderate shade earned 669 USD per hectare a year, 65% more than cocoa in full sun. We recorded a strong income gain. The number is in the quote. But shade was not assigned at random, fertiliser and care differed, and the spread is wide (plus or minus 565 vs 442). Approve keeps it. Reject: income for shaded tree crops drops from 'moderate positive' to 'mixed evidence'. AI's view: The quote matches what we recorded; the weak comparison is noted in the record, and these field surveys are within our rules.

units.quote:
The agroforestry system retains
15% more water in the soil in the driest
month (April) than the slash-and-burn
system (8% humidity in a traditional field
and 23% in a Quesungual field). This
difference is equivalent to 20mm of
rainfall, which means that crops can be
sustained 20 more days without rainfall.
And it is this difference that counts for
the success or failure of a crop in a
climatic regime with irregular dry spells
during the rainy season. 
Besides better infiltration of rainwater
into the soil profile through the soil
cover, the increase in soil moisture can be
explained by the increase in organic
matter content of the soil.
